Shares of IBM (IBM) currently trade at 19.9 times earnings, while the S&P 500 sits at 21.9. Investors buying at that multiple need to understand the underlying assets, and the company has recently changed its messaging. During the fiscal Q2 2025 call, executives focused on a running total of generative AI business that they defined as their book of business. The most recent presentation offered a different focal point. So what is management talking up instead?

IBM Now Talks Up Recurring Software Revenue

Executives are now framing the company around reliable, repeating software revenue. During the fiscal Q2 2026 call on July 22, 2026, the company noted that about 80% of its annual software revenue is recurring. This division accounts for nearly 45% of total revenue.

A year prior, leadership anchored its pitch to a different metric. During the fiscal Q2 2025 call, the company reported its generative AI book of business stood at over $7.5 billion since inception. That figure climbed from over $3 billion during the fiscal Q3 2024 call. Highlighting a rapidly growing cumulative total gave investors a straightforward view into AI demand.

Generative AI remains part of the conversation. Management noted on the latest call that the technology represented about 50% of quarterly Consulting signings. Yet the company has stopped emphasizing the cumulative tally.

Software Is IBM's Largest Source Of Revenue

The software unit brought in $30.0 billion in fiscal 2025, accounting for 44% of the company's revenue over that period. Sales in the division expanded by 10.6%, compared with a 1.8% growth rate for Consulting, which is the second-largest business segment.

The company also tracks annual recurring revenue. Executives placed that metric at $24.6 billion during the most recent call, representing an 8% increase from a year earlier.

The generative AI metric measured a different type of performance: a cumulative book of business since inception. It never reflected actual yearly sales, whereas recurring software revenue provides an annual baseline.

Is IBM's Turn To Software Good News For You?

This strategic pivot toward software presents a more reassuring than concerning picture for investors, though it comes with a catch. A baseline of repeating revenue offers more stability than a lifetime tally of generative AI business, and this reliable income anchors the largest division at the company.

The complication is that software is also where IBM missed expectations during fiscal Q2 2026. Software revenue grew 5% for the quarter, but its organic growth was flat. Executives noted that tens of large deals failed to close on time, and that about a third of those delayed contracts had finalized by the earnings call.

title: Investors Are Paying More for Walmart Than Amazon. Here’s Why That Doesn’t Add Up.
detail:
Investors Are Paying More for Walmart Than Amazon. Here’s Why That Doesn’t Add Up.
Jabran Kundi

WMT
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Walmart Inc. (NASDAQ:WMT) has opened a fulfillment center of more than 900,000 square feet in Stockton, California. The site uses automation and machine learning to cut the usual 12-step order process down to five. It will also employ about 1,000 people. The company says its next-generation fulfillment centers, of which Stockton is the fifth, will enable it to reach 95% of the U.S. population with next-day or two-day shipping when combined with the rest of its network. The stock closed more than 2% higher on October 8, its fourth straight gain. Beyond its push for faster delivery, Walmart's defensive appeal remains a key attraction for investors. But which other companies joined WMT on our list of the 10 Best Bear Market Stocks to Invest In Right Now?

Investors Are Paying More for Walmart Than Amazon. Here's Why That Doesn't Add Up.
Automation Is Changing Walmart's Business

I believe Stockton is just one piece of a much bigger shift. Walmart's U.S. e-commerce sales have grown more than 20% for 10 straight quarters, and fast deliveries jumped 48% last quarter. CFO John David Rainey said much of Walmart's recent spending has gone into supply chain automation and speed. That spending is also lifting higher-margin businesses. Advertising rose 38% last quarter, and membership fee revenue hit a record. Faster delivery brings more shoppers online, which feeds those businesses.

Still, Walmart remains a retailer at heart. Its stock fell 9% after its August report, despite beating estimates and raising its outlook. The decline reflected slow comparable sales and a soft Q3 guide, with operating income expected to grow just 2% to 4% as Walmart puts tariff refunds back into lower prices. Walmart's short-term margin pressure hasn't stopped hedge funds from backing the retail giant. See why WMT ranks No. 3 among the 10 Best Dividend Kings to Buy According to Hedge Funds and which other stocks made the list?

Walmart Costs More Than Amazon

Walmart's stock trades at a premium to its historical norms. The forward non-GAAP P/E of 37.48x sits about 24% above its 5-year average. That's even higher than Amazon, which trades at about 31x despite also owning AWS, a fast-growing, high-margin cloud business. The forward Price-to-sales ratio of 1.14x is also about 28% above its average. Yet analysts expect EPS to grow only 9% this fiscal year, about 12% in each of the next two, and 7% in fiscal 2030. Even based on fiscal 2030 earnings, the P/E would be around 28x. As of July 31, Walmart carried approximately $38.9 billion in net debt, excluding lease obligations. In my view, the automation story is big, but the stock already prices in a lot of it.

Netflix (NFLX) stock has dropped 12% since mid-September, retreating from a recent high of $80.32. When a familiar company discounts this quickly, investors often look for an entry point before the price rebounds. Yet this selloff has a reason behind it, and Netflix has navigated sharp declines before. So what pushed the stock down, and has buying Netflix after its sharp falls paid before?

Why Did Netflix Stock Fall?

Netflix stock had already slipped from its September 14 high when Wells Fargo analysts downgraded the shares on September 18, and it fell further that day. The analysts warned that weaker engagement and content could pressure margins and valuation.

Internal figures illustrate how slowly viewing is growing. During the July 16 call, management noted that view hours grew 2% in the first half of 2026, compared with 1.5% in 2025. A co-CEO has since acknowledged publicly that the company is not growing as fast as he wants.

Did Netflix Reward Investors Who Bought Earlier Declines?

History suggests the strategy often works, and Netflix offers a substantial sample size to evaluate. Since 2010, the stock has fallen 20% or more within 30 trading days on 16 separate occasions. Today's fall is smaller: Netflix is 12% below its September 14 high. All but the two drops from 2026 have a full year of subsequent trading data. The shares traded higher twelve months later in 10 of those 14 older occurrences. At the median, a $10,000 investment made on the day of the drop was worth about $14,100 a year later.

Investors stepping in during these selloffs usually faced further losses before seeing a return. At the median, the stock fell another 17% after the initial drop. In 7 of the 16 drops, the shares fell at least a fifth further. The steepest loss followed the August 2011 decline, leaving a buyer down 72% a year later. Even successful trades required patience: the best price over the following year arrived a median of 287 days after the drop, or about nine months.

title: If Palantir Stock Looks Expensive, You Need To Read This
detail:
If Palantir Stock Looks Expensive, You Need To Read This

Image from Pixabay

Shares of Palantir Technologies (PLTR) currently trade at 137.7 times its adjusted earnings over the past twelve months, a metric that adds stock-based pay back after tax. Paying that multiple for a single year of profit appears steep, yet the valuation shifts when measured against the next two years. The following breakdown highlights what investors are actually paying for the profit Palantir is expected to generate over those two years.

How Much You Pay For Palantir's Coming Earnings

Based on the consensus forecast for fiscal 2026, which concludes this December, Palantir trades at 121.5 times earnings. Looking further ahead to the forecast for fiscal 2027, the valuation falls to 81.7 times. Both figures offer a stark contrast to the 137.7 multiple applied to the past twelve months.

The share price remains constant across all three calculations, and only the underlying profit estimates change. Palantir earned $3.7 billion on that adjusted basis over the past twelve months. Projections call for the company to earn $4.1 billion in fiscal 2026 and $6.2 billion in fiscal 2027.

Palantir Has To Grow Revenue By Half

Hitting those targets requires Palantir to maintain rapid expansion, even if the pace slows from its current trajectory. The consensus forecast indicates sales will rise 50.2% from fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2027, reaching $12.3 billion. Projected profit increases 48.6% on the same forecast, tracking almost in step with sales and assuming no wider margin between the two years.

Palantir is currently growing at a faster clip. Sales climbed 78.9% over the past twelve months, and rose 92.8% in the latest quarter compared to a year earlier. During the company's August 3, 2026 call, management noted immense demand from enterprises for sovereign AI.

The consensus sales forecast for fiscal 2026 aligns closely with internal guidance. Management used that same call to raise its full-year sales guidance to a range between $8.150 billion and $8.158 billion. The current forecast sits just 0.7% above the midpoint of that range.

Palantir Needs Fat Profits And One Market To Last

The profit margin represents the most likely area where Palantir could fall short of expectations. The consensus forecast models Palantir keeping 50% of its sales as net profit in fiscal 2026, compared to 43% in fiscal 2025, the last full year it reported. Palantir kept 49% of its sales as net profit over the past twelve months, so the forecast asks it to hold that level for a full year. Management also warned on the August call that it expected a significant ramp in expenses in the third quarter, because of the seasonal timing of new hires. That quarter has ended, and Palantir has not yet reported its results. Costs that rise faster than sales would bring the forecast profit down.

title: Is Snowflake Stock Riskier Than It Looks?
detail:
Is Snowflake Stock Riskier Than It Looks?
Trefis Team
Tue, October 13, 2026 at 1:12 PM MDT 3 min read
SNOW
^GSPC
MSFT
AMZN
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Snowflake (SNOW) stock has returned 169% over the past six months, against 14.0% for the S&P 500. Investors appear to believe artificial intelligence has put the company on a faster growth track, and the latest quarter supports that view. Yet on the most recent earnings call, executives pointed out a catch in the AI business. So what is the catch?

What Did Snowflake's Management Flag About AI?

Executives said Snowflake earns less on its AI sales than on the rest of its product lineup. During the fiscal Q2 2027 call on September 2, 2026, the company lowered its fiscal 2027 forecast for adjusted product gross margin to 74%, from 75% on the prior call. Management cited a larger share of sales coming from fast-growing AI workloads, where the contribution margin is lower today.

AI represents a major source of that new growth. Product revenue growth accelerated to 37% year over year in fiscal Q2 2027, and executives noted that AI products contributed about half of that acceleration. Adoption is spreading quickly, as CoWork, one of Snowflake's AI products, expanded to reach 5,800 total accounts in the quarter. So the faster the AI business expands, the more of Snowflake's sales come at a thinner margin.

Snowflake Depends On Product Revenue For 95% Of Sales

Product revenue reached $4.5 billion in fiscal 2026, up 29.2% from the prior year. That segment makes up 95% of Snowflake's total revenue, and the AI workloads are sold directly inside it. The thinner margin on AI therefore sits inside Snowflake's main business, not in a side project.

Current valuations leave little room for that. Snowflake trades at 23.2 times its sales, compared with 3.1 for the S&P 500. The stock also sits just 2.3% below its high for the past year. Yet the company lost money over the past twelve months, so a price-to-earnings ratio is not meaningful. The net margin was negative 20.1%, against a profit of 13.3% for the broader index.

The share price appears to assume that rapid growth will translate into profit. Management noted the company remains on track for a GAAP profit in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2028. However, with a thinner margin on AI sales, Snowflake has less to work with on the way there.

Is Snowflake's Profit Plan Holding Up So Far?

So far, executives say the plan is intact. On the same call, management raised the fiscal 2027 forecast for adjusted operating margin to 14.5%, up from 13.5%. The company stated it is offsetting growing cloud costs with slowing headcount expense. This protects the operating margin, but it is not the same as AI sales becoming more profitable on their own.
